claims.claim_text: The standard itself is thinner than its reputation: it defines a signal layer and a state machine into which bits are shifted through a shift register, after which commands are run inside the device.
claims.quote_verbatim: JTAG is mostly just a signal layer definition
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski

claims.claim_text: What those commands mean is not part of it. The set the state machine interprets depends on the device attached, which is why a given debugger supports particular processor families rather than everything with the connector.
claims.quote_verbatim: the amount of commands that the state machine then interprets is depending on the device
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski

claims.claim_text: For one large processor family the layers above are pinned down by a separate specification, the vendor's debug interface document, and that is what a probe has to implement to be useful.
claims.quote_verbatim: all that stuff is defined by the ARM debug interface version 5
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski

claims.claim_text: The transport is close to interchangeable at that level: whether the physical link is the four-wire interface or the two-wire one, the commands running over it are much the same.
claims.quote_verbatim: the commands that are running on top of that are pretty much the same
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski

claims.claim_text: The two-wire variant generally uses a subset of the same pins, which is why boards often expose one or the other from the same footprint.
claims.quote_verbatim: there is singleware debug, which is, you know, it's usually a subset of the pins
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The cleanest description of a debug probe is therefore a translator: it converts the debugger's remote protocol into commands on the wire.
claims.quote_verbatim: it is a GDB remote protocol to JTAG converter
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski

claims.claim_text: That translation is chattier than it looks. Every single step issues a stream of commands, because each watched variable must be located and read back out of memory over the link before it can be displayed.
claims.quote_verbatim: GDB itself actually is issuing a lot of commands with every step
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Knowing that is what makes the interface clock rate a real decision rather than a default — you trade link speed against reliability depending on how much data you need to move.
claims.quote_verbatim: even like selected your JTAG speed, you might be more or less willing to slow it down
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The mental model that clears up most of the confusion is that all of it is reading and writing registers, and that programming a part is only one of the things this allows.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's actually just like reading and writing registers in order to program a chip
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The debug block sits immediately beside the processor on the die, which is why access to it means control of the processor and the ability to read all of memory.
claims.quote_verbatim: You're, you're controlling the processor and you're able to read all the memory.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The name records the original purpose: the T is for test, not for programming.
claims.quote_verbatim: hence the name joint test and action group
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Boundary scan is that purpose in practice — it reads the input and output pins of the device directly.
claims.quote_verbatim: Boundary scan allows you to actually read the, directly read all the IO pins.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: For a thousand-pin ball grid array with no X-ray equipment available, that is how you confirm every ball actually landed on its pad and is not shorted to its neighbour.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can make sure that your thousand pin BGA, that every one of those pins is actually connected to the ball
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: It has limits: the scan operates far too slowly to exercise something like a high-speed memory bus.
claims.quote_verbatim: You're not going to control a DDR3 memory bus or something like that.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Designing test coverage onto the chain moves effort earlier — fewer physical test points are needed on the board — but the handling problem does not disappear, since jigs, contacts and board flow through production still have to be engineered.
claims.quote_verbatim: maybe you move it all to be on a JTAG chain, right? So maybe you don't need as many test points
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Get Smart About Automation - Caducous Cyborg Concerns

claims.claim_text: Chaining across a panel lets programming run through a single breakout rather than a bed of contacts, which matters because a panel of ten or twenty boards can need hundreds of spring pins and one that fails to make contact fails the panel.
claims.quote_verbatim: pogo pins can be a pain in the ass because if you've got a big panel
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Motors And Upgrading Sinclairs - Adapting Apraxiated Automobiles

claims.claim_text: As a handoff boundary between a hardware contractor and a client's firmware team, it is a natural stopping point: check the supply rails, confirm the parts can be scanned, and pass the boards on.
claims.quote_verbatim: we'll just test the voltage rails test that we can JTAG scan the chips
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Nearly every low-cost debugger, commercial or hobbyist, is built around the same dual-channel USB interface chip, so the only real difference between them is the buffer logic in front that handles voltage translation.
claims.quote_verbatim: the only difference amongst manufacturers' programmers that use this chip is the buffer logic on the front
claims.speaker: Ian Lesnet
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Lesnet - Bus Buccaneer Builder

claims.claim_text: Making that buffer logic programmable turns one board into many: putting a programmable logic device in the buffer position and wiring its own debug connection to the interface chip's second channel means an entirely new programmer personality can be uploaded over USB.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can, over USB, upload an entirely new programmer logic into the CPLD on the fly
claims.speaker: Ian Lesnet
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Lesnet - Bus Buccaneer Builder

claims.claim_text: The same programmable part earns its place a second time by participating in the board's self-test.
claims.quote_verbatim: that CPLD is able to help out with the self-test
claims.speaker: Ian Lesnet
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Lesnet - Bus Buccaneer Builder

claims.claim_text: A product whose behaviour lives in the host software and not the hardware is also the cheapest to support, which is a design argument as much as a business one.
claims.quote_verbatim: the one that requires the least amount of support
claims.speaker: Ian Lesnet
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Lesnet - Bus Buccaneer Builder

claims.claim_text: A well-equipped probe does more than talk to the core: powering the target from the interface's reference pin, driven by a command from the debugger, removes a separate supply from the bench.
claims.quote_verbatim: it will power your target using the power reference pin of the JTAG interface
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski

claims.claim_text: Folding a serial adapter into the same board means one plug gives both debug control and a console, which is more useful in practice than it sounds.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can just plug it in and have serial while you also have JTAG or SWD
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski

claims.claim_text: A bootloader that works over this interface can avoid taxing the target: a small separate chip loads a snippet of code into the target's RAM to execute, so no program memory is consumed and there is no shared space for the application and the loader to corrupt.
claims.quote_verbatim: it doesn't occupy any memory on the target chip
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski

claims.claim_text: Whether the interface is brought out at all decides which boards can be used this way; a popular development board's omission of it was reason enough to design a different one.
claims.quote_verbatim: The problem is it doesn't have the JTAC interface exposed.
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski

claims.claim_text: Semihosting inverts the usual direction of debug: the application raises a hardware exception, the debugger catches it and performs the operation on the host, so target code can print, open and read files that exist on the development machine.
claims.quote_verbatim: there is so-called semi-hosting
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski

claims.claim_text: That is the practical route to getting bulk test data into a device with no storage card and no other interface, when the debug link is already present for flashing firmware.
claims.quote_verbatim: you don't have an SD card, you don't have an interface, but you have JTAG
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski

claims.claim_text: Acquiring a real debugger is the step past a beginner platform: the processor underneath is capable, and the debugger is what lets you use the space and speed the friendly environment was hiding.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm going to buy a JTAG. And now you've got a platform to do really cool stuff.
claims.speaker: Elecia White
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Elecia White - Wirewove Worshipping Wookieist?

claims.claim_text: Two probes can debug two targets simultaneously without virtual machines, though pairing two identical processors is usually the wrong architecture when a faster single one would do.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can dual debug using two JTAG modules
claims.speaker: Elecia White
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Elecia White - Wirewove Worshipping Wookieist?

claims.claim_text: Documentation for how to attach a debugger belongs in the source tree rather than in posts elsewhere, because when the implementation changes the external article goes stale while remaining the first thing people find.
claims.quote_verbatim: then you essentially have an old article, which isn't up to date anymore, but which still turns up
claims.speaker: Jeroen Domburg

claims.claim_text: A development board that puts a dual-channel USB interface chip on board and wires one channel as the programmer removes the need to buy the vendor's own programming pod.
claims.quote_verbatim: one of the channels is connected as, uh, the JTAG programmer
claims.speaker: Dmitry Nedospasov

claims.claim_text: Building the programmer itself, a small microcontroller can beat programmable logic on cost and part count: one needs only a regulator and decoupling capacitors, and its clock can be trimmed on the fly from the synchronisation packets on the USB wire.
claims.quote_verbatim: this particular PIC microcontroller can adjust its clock based on the synchronization packets coming over the USB wires
claims.speaker: Luke Valenty

claims.claim_text: Programmable logic loses that comparison because the small parts lack integrated regulators and cannot adjust a clock finely enough to track a host, so an external oscillator is required.
claims.quote_verbatim: you don't have a fine enough adjustment of the clock to be able to do something like that
claims.speaker: Luke Valenty

claims.claim_text: Testing a programmable logic device is not a matter of powering a few pins and attaching a probe — it effectively needs the whole board, with rails brought up in the right order and substantial current on the low-voltage core supply.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't just power a few pins and throw a JTAG on there
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Craig J Bishop

claims.claim_text: On parts that combine processors with fabric the boot order inverts the usual expectation: the processors come up first and are what bring up the fabric, so debug access to the processor side comes first and everything else follows from there.
claims.quote_verbatim: So you get JTAG access to the ARM side first, and boot up the ARM processors
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Craig J Bishop

claims.claim_text: Silicon cannot be breakpointed after fabrication, so the observability has to be designed in beforehand — which in one project meant spending the last two weeks before tape-out building the on-chip debug infrastructure.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can't put breakpoints there. It's crystal. It's done.
claims.speaker: Julia Desmazes
claims.episode_title: Chip Design for Fun (and Waffles) with Julia Desmazes

claims.claim_text: Building that interface yourself rather than dropping in an existing open core is defensible as a learning strategy, and it pays off when the design later needs a capability the existing hardware does not have.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's why I'm going to rebuild it myself in order to fully understand that
claims.speaker: Julia Desmazes
claims.episode_title: Chip Design for Fun (and Waffles) with Julia Desmazes

claims.claim_text: It also exposes what you did not know: a design that simulated correctly against its own test benches failed the moment a real commercial probe was connected, which is the point at which the wrong assumption becomes visible.
claims.quote_verbatim: I plugged the actual JTAG probe there and it doesn't work
claims.speaker: Julia Desmazes
claims.episode_title: Chip Design for Fun (and Waffles) with Julia Desmazes

claims.claim_text: Once the specification is genuinely understood, custom features can be added to the interface for whatever the particular hardware needs, and debugging becomes an iteration on the debug interface itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: I know that I can add custom features to JTAG which are going to be useful for debugging my weird hardware
claims.speaker: Julia Desmazes
claims.episode_title: Chip Design for Fun (and Waffles) with Julia Desmazes

claims.claim_text: Verifying such a block in programmable logic means instantiating both the design and the interface, routing the interface out to spare pins, and driving it with a second, known-good device to confirm the data is flowing.
claims.quote_verbatim: I stuck a second JTAG
claims.speaker: Julia Desmazes
claims.episode_title: Chip Design for Fun (and Waffles) with Julia Desmazes

claims.claim_text: The interface can also rescue a finished part: a test pin exposed on a chip allowed a flip-flop that powered up in a random state — a fault that had not appeared in simulation — to be forced before the master reset, saving the mask set.
claims.quote_verbatim: I just toggled the test pin before my master reset
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Carnassial Chip Chemicals

claims.claim_text: As an attack path this is well understood: debug control of the processor is the whole point of the interface, and a small board replaying a stored command file can be plugged in and left to run.
claims.quote_verbatim: You hook it up, you get debug control over a CPU.
claims.speaker: Joe Fitzpatrick

claims.claim_text: The command file itself is a standard artefact — a serial vector format file is just a series of interface commands — and replaying one can modify memory to change something as consequential as a root password.
claims.quote_verbatim: that series of JTAG commands could modify memory to change a root password
claims.speaker: Joe Fitzpatrick

claims.claim_text: The physical opening is often an accessory slot: removing an expansion module from an industrial controller exposed a ten-pin header, and a small board plugged in there took power from the connector, waited, halted the processor and wrote a pin to change the controller's output.
claims.quote_verbatim: it waits five seconds, it halts the CPU and writes to a GPIO to turn off your output
claims.speaker: Joe Fitzpatrick

claims.claim_text: Nothing about that required firmware analysis. A sample of the same model bought openly identifies the processor and base firmware, and tracing the board maps each controlled pin to a physical output.
claims.quote_verbatim: I can reverse engineer the board and see where the GPIOs are connected
claims.speaker: Joe Fitzpatrick

claims.claim_text: Defensive practice has moved in response: within a few years vendors stopped labelling debug and serial test points, disabled the consoles and locked the interface on shipped devices.
claims.quote_verbatim: vendors have stopped obviously marking JTAG and UART test points
claims.speaker: Joe Fitzpatrick

claims.claim_text: Integration does more than any of those measures — as functionality collapses into one or two pieces of silicon with no test points, board-level access ceases to be the route in and attacks have to move to the silicon itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: so much of the functionality is integrated into a single piece of silicon
claims.speaker: Joe Fitzpatrick

claims.claim_text: The equilibrium argument follows from that: attention moves to whatever is cheapest to attack, so improving software pushes effort towards hardware, improving hardware pushes it towards silicon, and beyond that towards people.
claims.quote_verbatim: anybody who really wants to get into a system is going to look for the cheapest spot
claims.speaker: Joe Fitzpatrick

claims.claim_text: The common glitching target is the boot sequence: the device reads a configuration fuse and, depending on it, enables the debug lock, so disturbing the part at exactly that moment can skip the step and the device comes up unlocked.
claims.quote_verbatim: if like at the right time you skip over, turning on the J tag lock, it just comes up on lock
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Shouting at chips with Colin O'Flynn

claims.claim_text: Once that has happened the rest is undramatic — with debug access the memory can simply be read out.
claims.quote_verbatim: from having J tag access, you can just go and peek and poke at memory and just pull it all out
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Shouting at chips with Colin O'Flynn

claims.claim_text: The port is also a side-channel measurement point. Because propagation delay through a device varies with supply voltage, timing jitter observed through the debug interface yields an accurate measure of the device's power consumption, and from that, information about secrets.
claims.quote_verbatim: the time delay varies with voltage, which means you can actually get a really accurate measurement of power
claims.speaker: Colin O'Flynn
claims.episode_title: Small Scale Electronics Manufacturing with Colin O'Flynn

claims.claim_text: Published security frameworks make this checkable rather than speculative: the lower levels are self-assessable checklists containing concrete items such as whether the debug port is locked, with worked threat models for particular product categories, while the highest level requires actual side-channel and fault-injection testing.
claims.quote_verbatim: the highest level involved actual side channel and fault injection testing
claims.speaker: Colin O'Flynn
claims.episode_title: Small Scale Electronics Manufacturing with Colin O'Flynn

claims.claim_text: Leaving the port open after programming is a named item on the standard weakness lists, and those lists are a reasonable starting point — the difficulty is never knowing what to do, it is implementing it.
claims.quote_verbatim: leaving your JTAG port just open
claims.speaker: Joe Grand
claims.episode_title: New Life Skills with Joe Grand

claims.claim_text: The gap between seeing test points on a board and using them is filled by a tool that identifies which unknown pins on an unpopulated connector form a debug interface, so identification and exploitation become two separate, tractable steps.
claims.quote_verbatim: a tool to help you identify the function of unknown test points
claims.speaker: Joe Grand
claims.episode_title: New Life Skills with Joe Grand

claims.claim_text: A further scan correlates each physical pin to its bit position within the boundary scan register, which is a probing aid for attackers and an engineering aid for everyone else.
claims.quote_verbatim: help you identify the physical pins on the chip and how they correspond to the actual boundary scan register
claims.speaker: Joe Grand
claims.episode_title: New Life Skills with Joe Grand

claims.claim_text: The tool deliberately stops there: it can drive an open-source debugger once an interface is found, but slowly, and the intended workflow is to switch to a proper probe afterwards.
claims.quote_verbatim: once you find the interface, you'll want to end up using proper, faster, better tools
claims.speaker: Joe Grand
claims.episode_title: New Life Skills with Joe Grand

claims.claim_text: Choosing an unusual microcontroller for an open project has a lasting cost in outside contributions, whatever its technical merits.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think I'd have more community contributions if it wasn't such an arcane kind of thing
claims.speaker: Joe Grand
claims.episode_title: New Life Skills with Joe Grand

claims.claim_text: The skills involved transfer directly back into ordinary engineering: dumping firmware, reading hex, finding the debug pins and probing around are the same motions used to debug one's own product.
claims.quote_verbatim: a lot of the skills to use in reverse engineering are also very useful for debugging
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An interview with Alvaro and Jen from the URE Podcast

claims.claim_text: For a system that will never be accessible again, the temptation to attach a debugger during bring-up is a trap. Anything learned that way is unavailable in flight, so each early problem should instead be answered by getting the relevant data into the telemetry stream already being consumed.
claims.quote_verbatim: figure out how you can get that data in the sort of data stream that you're already consuming
claims.speaker: Charles Aylward
claims.episode_title: Software for Rockets with Charles Aylward
